title: The commoner Roman view: original righteousness wholly unowed, so a state of pure nature was possible
source_text: XVII. Sed in diversum abit communior Doctorum Scholae Romanae sententia. Etenim existimant justitiam & sanctitatem, quae in primo homine fuit, non solum fuisse donum supernaturale, & quod ad naturam non ad gratiam pertinebat; sed etiam aliquid naturae humanae, quamvis innocenti & nondum peccatrici, prorsus indebitum: ita ut nihil repugnaret sapientiae, bonitati, & justitiae divinae hominem sine tali justitia creari. Unde est quod inter status hominis possibiles ponunt statum purae naturae, sive hominis, ut loquuntur, in puris naturalibus. In quo statu ex eorum mente, homo nec justus, nec injustus esset: nec ullius peccati reus nec etiam ulla gratia praeditus.
pass_a_gloss: But the more common opinion of the Doctors of the Roman School goes the other way. For they think that the justice and sanctity which was in the first man was not only a supernatural gift, and which pertained to nature not to grace [so the print; thesis XII has to grace not to nature]; but also something wholly unowed to human nature, though innocent and not yet sinful: so that nothing would conflict with divine wisdom, goodness, and justice if man were created without such justice. Whence it is that among the possible states of man they place the state of pure nature, or of man, as they speak, in pure naturals. In which state in their mind, man would be neither just, nor unjust: neither guilty of any sin nor also endowed with any grace.
pass_b_english: The more common view among the teachers of the Roman school goes another way. They hold that the righteousness and holiness of the first man was not only a supernatural gift, belonging to grace and not to nature, but also something wholly unowed to human nature, even innocent nature not yet sinful. So it would not have been at odds with God's wisdom, goodness and justice for man to be created without such righteousness.

That is why they count among man's possible states the state of pure nature, or, as they put it, of man in a purely natural condition. In that state, as they see it, man would be neither righteous nor unrighteous, neither guilty of any sin nor endowed with any grace.

choices.term: quod ad naturam non ad gratiam pertinebat
choices.english: belonging to grace and not to nature
choices.why: The print inverts the phrase of thesis XII (ad gratiam non ad naturam). A gift called supernatural in the same breath cannot belong to nature rather than grace, so Pass B follows the sense Le Blanc's argument requires and the note records the printed reading.
rejected: belonging to nature and not to grace
belonging (as the print has it) to nature and not to grace
